examples.question_text: A sample satisfies $\dfrac{dM}{dt}=-0.15M$, where $M$ is measured in grams and $t$ in hours. Initially, its mass is $160$ grams. Find its mass after $4$ hours, correct to $2$ decimal places.
examples.solution_text:
Use $M=Ae^{kt}$. The initial mass gives $A=160$, and $k=-0.15$.
$M=160e^{-0.15t}$
$\begin{aligned}M(4)&=160e^{-0.6}\\&=87.81\text{ g}\quad\text{(to 2 decimal places)}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: A culture satisfies $\dfrac{dN}{dt}=kN$. Its population is $600$ initially and $1200$ after $3$ hours. Find $k$ exactly, then predict its population after $9$ hours.
examples.solution_text:
The initial population gives $A=600$.
$\begin{aligned}600e^{3k}&=1200\\e^{3k}&=2\\3k&=\ln 2\\k&=\dfrac{\ln 2}{3}\text{ h}^{-1}\end{aligned}$
Use the exact value of $k$ in the prediction.
$\begin{aligned}N(9)&=600e^{9(\ln 2/3)}\\&=600e^{3\ln 2}\\&=600\times 8\\&=4800\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: A population follows $P=Ae^{kt}$, where $t$ is measured in years. It is $800$ when $t=2$ and $3200$ when $t=6$. Find $k$ and $A$ exactly.
examples.solution_text:
Divide the two data equations to eliminate $A$.
$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{Ae^{6k}}{Ae^{2k}}&=\dfrac{3200}{800}\\e^{4k}&=4\\4k&=\ln 4\\k&=\dfrac{\ln 2}{2}\text{ year}^{-1}\end{aligned}$
Substitute into the earlier data equation.
$\begin{aligned}Ae^{2(\ln 2/2)}&=800\\2A&=800\\A&=400\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text:
A quantity follows $Q=Ae^{0.1t}$, where $t$ is measured in hours. It is $240$ units when $t=5$.
(a) Find $A$, correct to $2$ decimal places.
(b) Find when the quantity reaches $720$ units, correct to $2$ decimal places.
examples.solution_text:
(a)
$\begin{aligned}Ae^{0.5}&=240\\A&=240e^{-0.5}\\&=145.57\text{ units}\quad\text{(to 2 decimal places)}\end{aligned}$
(b) Keep $A=240e^{-0.5}$ unrounded.
$\begin{aligned}240e^{-0.5}e^{0.1t}&=720\\e^{0.1t-0.5}&=3\\0.1t-0.5&=\ln 3\\t&=\dfrac{\ln 3+0.5}{0.1}\\&=15.99\text{ hours}\quad\text{(to 2 decimal places)}\end{aligned}$
The quantity reaches $720$ units after the given observation at $t=5$ hours.

examples.question_text:
(a) A substance satisfies $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=-0.04Q$, with $t$ in days. Find its half-life, correct to $2$ decimal places.
(b) A population satisfies $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.08P$, with $t$ in years. Find its doubling time, correct to $2$ decimal places.
(c) Another substance has a half-life of $6$ hours. Find its decay constant exactly, then find when only one eighth of its initial amount remains.
examples.solution_text:
(a) Set the amount equal to half its initial value.
$\begin{aligned}Ae^{-0.04t}&=\dfrac{A}{2}\\e^{-0.04t}&=\dfrac12\\-0.04t&=\ln\dfrac12\\t&=\dfrac{\ln 2}{0.04}\\&=17.33\text{ days}\quad\text{(to 2 decimal places)}\end{aligned}$
(b) Set the population equal to twice its initial value.
$\begin{aligned}Ae^{0.08t}&=2A\\e^{0.08t}&=2\\0.08t&=\ln 2\\t&=\dfrac{\ln 2}{0.08}\\&=8.66\text{ years}\quad\text{(to 2 decimal places)}\end{aligned}$
(c) Use the half-life to determine $k$.
$\begin{aligned}Ae^{6k}&=\dfrac A2\\e^{6k}&=\dfrac12\\6k&=-\ln 2\\k&=-\dfrac{\ln 2}{6}\text{ h}^{-1}\end{aligned}$
Now solve for the time when one eighth remains.
$\begin{aligned}Ae^{kt}&=\dfrac A8\\e^{kt}&=\dfrac18\\kt&=-3\ln 2\\t&=\dfrac{-3\ln 2}{-\ln 2/6}\\&=18\text{ hours}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text:
A chemical satisfies $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=kQ$, where $Q$ is measured in grams and $t$ in hours. Its mass is $960$ grams initially and $480$ grams after $4$ hours.
(a) Find $k$ exactly.
(b) Find the rate of change when $Q=240$ grams, correct to $2$ decimal places.
(c) Find the rate of change at $t=12$ hours, correct to $2$ decimal places.
examples.solution_text:
(a) The initial mass gives $Q=960e^{kt}$.
$\begin{aligned}960e^{4k}&=480\\e^{4k}&=\dfrac12\\4k&=-\ln 2\\k&=-\dfrac{\ln 2}{4}\text{ h}^{-1}\end{aligned}$
(b) Substitute the given mass directly into $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=kQ$.
$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dQ}{dt}&=-\dfrac{\ln 2}{4}\times240\\&=-60\ln 2\\&=-41.59\text{ g/h}\quad\text{(to 2 decimal places)}\end{aligned}$
The mass is decreasing at $41.59$ grams per hour.
(c) First find the mass at $t=12$.
$\begin{aligned}Q(12)&=960e^{-3\ln 2}\\&=120\text{ g}\end{aligned}$
Then use the proportional rate model.
$\begin{aligned}\left.\dfrac{dQ}{dt}\right|_{t=12}&=-\dfrac{\ln 2}{4}\times120\\&=-30\ln 2\\&=-20.79\text{ g/h}\quad\text{(to 2 decimal places)}\end{aligned}$
The mass is decreasing at $20.79$ grams per hour.

examples.derivation: The initial condition gives A=160 and the differential equation gives k=-0.15 per hour. M(4)=160e^(-0.6)=87.809861775… g, rounding to 87.81 g.
A=600. The later observation gives e^(3k)=1200/600=2, hence k=ln(2)/3 per hour. N(9)=600e^(3ln(2))=600×8=4800.
Dividing the observations gives e^(4k)=3200/800=4. Thus k=ln(4)/4=ln(2)/2 per year. Substitution into Ae^(2k)=800 gives 2A=800 and A=400.
Ae^0.5=240 gives A=240e^(-0.5)=145.567358331… units, rounding to 145.57 units. Using this exact A, Q=720 gives e^(0.1t-0.5)=3, so t=(ln(3)+0.5)/0.1=15.986122887… hours, rounding to 15.99 hours.

For halving, e^(-0.04t)=1/2 gives t=ln(2)/0.04=17.328679514… days, rounding to 17.33 days. For doubling, e^(0.08t)=2 gives t=ln(2)/0.08=8.664339757… years, rounding to 8.66 years. A six-hour half-life gives k=-ln(2)/6 per hour. Then e^(kt)=1/8 gives kt=-3ln(2), hence t=18 hours.

A=960 and e^(4k)=480/960=1/2 give k=-ln(2)/4 per hour. At Q=240, kQ=-60ln(2)=-41.588830834… g/h, rounding to -41.59 g/h. At t=12, Q=960e^(-3ln(2))=120 g, so kQ=-30ln(2)=-20.794415417… g/h, rounding to -20.79 g/h. Both negative rates correctly describe decreasing mass.
